# Getting Started {.unnumbered}

<!-- DK: Explain Cmd/Ctrl. -->

*You can never look at the data too much.* -- Mark Engerman

The world confronts us. Make decisions we must.

We do all of our data science in the cloud, using GitHub Codespaces with Visual Studio Code (VS Code).

In this chapter you will sign up for GitHub, create a Codespace, and learn about tutorials. Everything runs in your browser. You don't install anything on your own machine. Tutorials are the standard format we use for homework assignments. They allow you to work at your own pace

Your answers to the questions on this page save automatically in your browser, so you can close the page and come back later without losing anything. If you ever want to wipe them all and begin again, click the **Start Over** button in the right-hand sidebar. 

Start by telling us who you are. Your instructor might also ask you to fill in the "ID" field so that your work can be matched to a grading database. If not, leave the "ID" field blank. Fill in the fields below and click **Submit**. You can edit your answers. 

```{r}
#| label: student-information-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::student_info()
```

## How to take a screenshot {.unnumbered}

Many questions in this chapter ask you to paste a screenshot as proof that you did something. Take the screenshot first, then click into the question's answer box and paste it with `Ctrl + V` (Windows, Chromebook) or `Cmd + V` (Mac). There is no upload button. A preview of your screenshot appears in the box when it has worked. Then click **Submit Answer**.

The easiest way to acccomplsh this is to copy the screenshot to your clipboard, so that you can paste it right away:

* **Windows:** press `Windows + Shift + S`, then drag a box around what you want to capture. The screenshot is copied to your clipboard.

* **Mac:** press `Cmd + Control + Shift + 4`, then drag a box around what you want to capture. Adding `Control` is what copies the screenshot to your clipboard. Without it, `Cmd + Shift + 4` saves a file to your Desktop instead, which you cannot paste.

* **Chromebook:** press `Ctrl + Shift + Show windows` (the key with a rectangle and two lines on it), drag a box around what you want to capture, and click **Copy to clipboard** in the notification that appears.

The screenshot should capture enough of the screenthat we can confirm that you followed our instructions.

## GitHub {.unnumbered}

Click [here](https://github.com/) and sign up for a GitHub by using the green button. Use your school email address for this account, if you are a student. 

Useful [advice](https://happygitwithr.com/github-acct.html#username-advice) for choosing a username includes using your real name, so people know who they are dealing with and can guess or remember it easily; making sure it is something you would be comfortable showing a future boss; keeping it short, and making it as unique as possible in as few characters as you can. Finally, make it timeless by avoiding references to your current university, employer, or home town. 

Once you have signed up for GitHub and are signed in to GitHub, go to `github.com/` followed by your username, and click the **Overview** tab. Your screenshot should look similar to this.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "A screenshot of a GitHub profile page in a browser, on the Overview tab, with the address bar showing github.com followed by the username."
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/github-profile-example.png")
```

```{r}
#| label: github-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Paste a screenshot of the Overview tab of your GitHub profile, at github.com/[your username]. Make sure the address bar is visible.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE
)
```

The [GitHub Student Developer Pack](https://education.github.com/pack) provides all sorts of perks, but you must visit that page to turn on the benefits. It confirms your student status on the basis of you having an email account at your school. 

If you are a student, go to that page now, sign in, and apply for the benefits. When you finish, GitHub tells you that your application has been submitted. Your screenshot should look similar to this. (If you are not a student, skip this question.)

## A throwaway Codespace {.unnumbered}

You create a new Codespace using the `https://github.com/PPBDS/codespace-starter` repository. We refer to this repo as `codespace-starter`.

Go to [`https://github.com/PPBDS/codespace-starter`](https://github.com/PPBDS/codespace-starter).

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/cs-1.png")
```

This Codespace is for learning the platform, not for your permanent work.

GitHub gives every account 60 free Codespaces hours per month. Free hours are not infinite, however, so it is your responsibility to stop (and delete) Codespaces you are no longer using.

### Launching the Codespace {.unnumbered}

Click the green **Code** button at the top right of the repository page, switch to the **Codespaces** tab, and click **"Create codespace on main."**

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/new-1.png")
```

This will take a minute or so. Behind the scenes, GitHub is creating a virtual machine in the cloud with all the necessary tools for doing data science. That machine is called a "Codespace."

You may be asked: "Do you trust the authors of the files in this folder?"

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/trust.png")
```

Click to agree.

Once the process is done, a banner message appears announcing "✅  YOUR CODESPACE IS READY."

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/ready-message.png")
```

GitHub gives your Codespace a randomly generated name. Mine is "cuddly space giggle", but yours will be different. The name appears in four spots: the address bar of your browser, the box at the top center of VS Code, the top of the Explorer panel on the left, and the blue button at the bottom left.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "A screenshot of a new Codespace in the browser, with the name 'cuddly space giggle' appearing in the address bar, in the box at the top center of VS Code, at the top of the Explorer panel, and in the blue button at the bottom left."

```

```{r}
#| label: launching-the-codespace-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Paste a screenshot of your browser window showing your own Codespace's name in at least one location.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE

```

### Touring the workspace {.unnumbered}

VS Code is an integrated development environment (IDE) for coding and data science. Highlights:

* This Codespace is in the cloud. The URL will be a combination of the GitHub-determined human-readable but somewhat nonsensical name — `cuddly space giggle` in my case — and a bunch of letters and numbers. There is no need to remember this URL. GitHub keeps track of things. You can see all your current Codespaces at [`https://github.com/codespaces`](https://github.com/codespaces).

* In the upper right-hand corner are the "Customize Layout ..." buttons. These are part of the VS Code "Title Bar." Since we aren't using the AI tools right now, it often makes sense to close the "Chat" window, which appears on the right side of the screen. You can close this in two ways: Click the "X" mark or click the "Toggle Secondary Side Bar" button, the furthest right-hand button. You can then bring the Chat window back by clicking the "Toggle Secondary Side Bar" button again. Try it now.

<!-- DK: They won't try it without a demand for a screenshot! -->

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/chat-buttons-cs.png")
```

* The "Activity Bar" is the narrow vertical strip on the far left with icons for Explorer, Search, Source Control, Extensions, etc. 

* The "Editor" is the large central area where you edit files.

* The "Panel" is the horizontal area below the Editor, containing the Problems, Output, Debug Console, Terminal, and Ports views. Our main focus is the Terminal view. This is where we "talk" to both the (cloud) computer itself and to the R program that it provides.

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/ready-message.png")
```

You can start new bash Terminals by clicking on the `+` sign above the list of terminals. Do so now. As you can see below, you now have two bash Terminals. You switch by selecting the one you want to work with from the list. You can type commands at the "prompt," which is where the red arrow is pointing below. 

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/t2.png")
```

If you hover your cursor over the terminal list, a split-screen and a trash can appear. Clicking on the trash can will close the terminal.

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/can.png")
```


The language can be a little confusing. There is a capital T "Terminal" view, which is one of the tabs across the top of the Panel. In that Terminal view, we can work with many individual small T "terminals" of various sorts. So far, you have only seen bash Terminals, which get a capital T because they are a type of named terminal. The bash shell is a program that lets you "talk" to the computer itself.

In addition to bash Terminals, we can also start an R session under the Terminal. Instead of clicking the `+` sign, click the small downward-pointing arrow next to it. This will show a variety of options.

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/cs-6.png")
```

Select "R Terminal." This will start an R session that lets you "talk" to R in the same way that a bash shell allows you to talk to the computer.

Click on the "R Interactive" tab which should appear beneath the other terminals on the right side of the Panel.

Type in `2 + 2` at the R prompt and hit `enter` (Windows) or `return` (Mac). (Going forward we will just use `Enter` to refer to this action. Mac users should hit `return`.)

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/t3.png")
```

An IDE like VS Code is designed to help us organize our work. We need to talk to the computer via the bash Terminal (a terminal running the bash shell), talk to R, view plots, and so on.

At the R Terminal, run `plot(1:10)`. We use the terms "run" and "execute" interchangeably. They both indicate that you should type the command at the appropriate terminal and hit `Enter`.

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/t4.png")
```

Data scientists make lots of plots.

```{r}

#| echo: false

  "Paste a screenshot of the plot you created with `plot(1:10)`.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE

```



Click into the bash Terminal, type `pwd`, and then press `Enter`. 

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/pwd.png")
```

**C**opy and **P**aste both the **C**ommand *and* the **R**esponse from the bash Terminal into the box below. We abbreviate this instruction as **CP**/**CR**.

```{r}
#| label: the-getting-started-exercises-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Paste, into the box below, both the command you ran and the response the bash Terminal printed.",
  type = "reflection"
)
```

We typically provide example answers, like the one below, after you submit your own response. Do not be concerned if your answer differs from the example we show.

````
codespace-starter $ pwd
/workspaces/codespace-starter
codespace-starter $
````

Also, we generally do not allow you to edit answers once you have submitted them. If you make a mistake, don't worry! Tutorials are graded Pass/Fail. 

`pwd` stands for **p**rint **w**orking **d**irectory: it shows the directory in which the terminal is working. The response confirms that you are inside your Codespace, a complete computer running in the cloud. It is OK if your formatting differs from ours. What matters is that you show that you ran the command as instructed.

That is the usual process: run something in a terminal, copy the command and the response, paste them into the answer box. Almost every exercise in every later tutorial works this way.

### Stopping, restarting and deleting the Codespace {.unnumbered}

A Codespace is your responsibility in the same way that your laptop is your responsibility. While a Codespace is running it counts against your free hours. An unused Codespace will be deleted by GitHub after 30 days.

There are three common ways to close a Codespace.

First, just leave it alone. GitHub will close it on its own after 30 minutes of inactivity, though we recommend changing that default to 15 minutes in your [Codespaces settings](https://github.com/settings/codespaces).

Second, type `Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + P`. The Command Palette provides access to all VS Code commands. Type `stop` into the search bar.

On some browsers, the keyboard shortcut does not work. You can always access the Command Palette by clicking the search bar at the top of the window and typing `>` followed by key words from the command you would like to use.

<!-- DK: Update the image. -->

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/command-palette.png")
```

Select "Codespaces: Stop Current Codespace."

Third, you can go to your personal Codespaces control panel at [`https://github.com/codespaces`](https://github.com/codespaces). You can also reach this page from any page on GitHub by clicking the menu icon in the upper left and selecting "Codespaces":

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/t7.png")
```

Which brings up this lst of options. Select "Codespaces."

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/t8.png")
```

Your main Codespaces page should look something like this:

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/codespaces-1.png")
```

This shows all your Codespaces, both active and inactive. The `...` menu on each row provides several commands, including "Stop Codespace."

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/codespaces-2.png")
```

Simply closing the browser window *does not* stop your Codespace from running. Always stop a Codespace explicitly to preserve your free hours.

Now stop this Codespace using whichever method you prefer.

Once it is stopped, you can restart it from your [Codespaces page](https://github.com/codespaces) by clicking the `...` menu next to this Codespace and then selecting **Open in Browser**.

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/codespaces-3.png")
```

Once you are done with a Codespace, you should **delete it.** To do so, go to your [Codespaces page](https://github.com/codespaces), click the `...` menu next to this Codespace and select **Delete**.

This Codespace was a sandbox. You do not own [`PPBDS/codespace-starter`](https://github.com/PPBDS/codespace-starter), so there is nowhere for your work to go once you stop using the Codespace. That is fine — you have already downloaded your answers, which is the only thing here worth keeping.

Delete your Codespace now. When you do, GitHub shows a message at the top of your Codespaces page confirming that it was deleted. Your screenshot should look similar to this.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "A screenshot of the top of the GitHub Codespaces page with a light blue banner reading: Codespace cuddly space giggle deleted."
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/codespace-deleted-example.png")
```

## Using your own machine

You can do all of this work on your own laptop, if you prefer. But, in that case, you are responsible for setting everything up. That means installing VS Code, Git and R. Ask your favorite AI to take a look at the `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` file from [`PPBDS/codespace-starter`](https://github.com/PPBDS/codespace-starter). The AI will then give you good advice as to the steps to take.You may also find it useful to use the same VS settings which are defined there.

You will also need to install, by hand, various R packages. From the R Terminal, you would run commands like:

```
install.packages("pak")
```

You may be asked to select a CRAN mirror. It does not matter which you choose.

```
pak::pak("tidyverse")
pak::pak("PPBDS/vscode.tutorials")
```

These steps are not enough to perfectly replicate what we show in the Codespace. See `PPBDS/devcontainers` for more details. But this should be enough to get you started, should you decide to go this route. 

## Start a tutorial {.unnumbered}

This section shows you how to start a tutorial. 

Create another Codespace, exactly as you did in the "Launching the Codespace" section above.

Once your Codespace is ready, look at the Activity Bar, the narrow vertical strip of icons on the far left. Hover over the icons until you find the one labeled **R Tutorials**, near the bottom, and click it. This lists the R packages that have tutorials. Click the package named **[vscode.tutorials](https://ppbds.github.io/vscode.tutorials/)** to see its tutorials.

Find the tutorial named **Orientation**. Hover over its name and click the sideways triangle button that appears. Doing so starts the tutorial.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "The R Tutorials panel in VS Code, listing tutorial packages. The vscode.tutorials package is expanded, with Orientation at the top of its tutorials and a play button next to it."
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/r-tutorials-orientation.png")
```

A new terminal named "R Tutorial" appears in the Panel.

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/t2.png")
```

The tutorial should automatically open in your browser. 

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("getting-started/images/t3.png")
```

Note how the web address includes `cuddly-space-giggle`, the GitHub name for my Codespace. The tutorial is running in the Codespace, viewable via my browser.

If the tutorial does not open automatically, hover over the web address in the "R Tutorial" terminal and press `Ctrl + Click` (Windows, Chromebook) or `Cmd + Click` (Mac).

You do not need to finish the Orientation tutorial now. After you finish, and download your answer, you should stop that Codespace and delete it.
